Monitoring-based rewards enhance learning performance and metacognitive monitoring accuracy (PMC)
mechanisms: A reward is read through its effect on perceived competence and self-determination: the interpersonal climate determines whether it feels informational or controlling, which in turn grows or erodes intrinsic motivation.
Tangible rewards are experienced as controlling and decrease intrinsic motivation, but the damage is moderated by contingency type, unexpectedness, and whether the reward also affirms competence.

Immediate payoffs motivate present-oriented students to work harder, but the external incentive can crowd out internal motivation, especially when the reward is large — the effect dampens, rather than amplifies, for students facing a higher marginal cost of effort.

Performance-contingent rewards heighten anxiety and trigger superficial learning, causing students to avoid challenge; decoupling the reward from performance and tying it to metacognitive accuracy restores a sense of control and preserves intrinsic motivation.
Accurate metacognitive monitoring improves resource allocation and deep processing; rewards aligned with monitoring accuracy sustain attention and reduce anxiety, enhancing learning performance.
objection_patterns: Does this reward make me feel controlled or does it affirm my competence?
Will this incentive crowd out the enjoyment I already get from the task?
Does the payoff arrive soon enough to matter, or is the future benefit still too distant?
Does this reward punish me for trying something difficult, pushing me toward safer, shallower work?
confidence: Meta-analytic and experimental evidence from education settings; mechanisms are robust across contexts, but precise magnitudes and long-run persistence of crowding effects remain uncertain.
